qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with painless haematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a flat area of mucosal reddening without an intraluminal mass. Biopsy shows cytologically malignant cells within a flat urothelium. If left untreated, what is the approximate risk of this lesion progressing to invasive cancer?
qs.e: Carcinoma in situ (CIS) is a flat urothelial malignancy that progresses to invasive cancer in 50–75% of untreated cases. Lower percentages are not supported by the data for CIS progression.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old woman from an area endemic for urinary schistosomiasis presents with haematuria. Which histologic type of bladder carcinoma is most likely to be found?
qs.e: Squamous cell carcinoma is common in areas where urinary schistosomiasis is endemic, arising from chronic irritation and squamous metaplasia. Urothelial carcinoma is the most common type globally but not specifically linked to schistosomiasis.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man presents with haematuria. Cystoscopy shows a papillary lesion. Biopsy reveals orderly architecture, low-grade cytologic atypia, and cohesive cells with maintained polarity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma is characterized by orderly architecture, low-grade atypia, and cohesive cells. High-grade carcinoma shows dyscohesion, significant atypia, and architectural disarray.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with haematuria. Biopsy of a bladder lesion reveals adenocarcinoma. Which of the following is a known origin for this tumour type?
qs.e: Bladder adenocarcinoma can arise from urachal remnants or extensive intestinal metaplasia. Schistosomiasis is associated with squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 65-year-old man presents with painless gross haematuria. Cystoscopy reveals a large papillary mass, and biopsy demonstrates dyscohesive cells, marked nuclear pleomorphism, and frequent atypical mitoses. What is the clinical implication of this high-grade histologic finding?
o: Indolent behaviour with minimal metastatic risk
High rate of progression to muscle-invasive cancer
qs.e: High-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma carries a high rate of progression to muscle-invasive cancer and significant metastatic potential. Low-grade papillary tumors, by contrast, rarely progress to invasive disease.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with haematuria. Biopsy reveals a tumour with deceptively bland cytology but invasive behaviour. Which variant of urothelial carcinoma is this most likely to be?
o: Sarcomatoid carcinoma of the urinary tract
qs.e: The nested variant of urothelial carcinoma is characterized by deceptively bland cytology despite its invasive nature. Sarcomatoid carcinoma is a distinct high-grade variant with spindle cells.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer & Urothelial Neoplasms: Types, Risks, Pathogenesis: MCQs

qs.q: A 5-year-old child presents with palpable purpura on the lower extremities, colicky abdominal pain, and haematuria. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
qs.e: Henoch-Schönlein purpura characteristically presents with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and renal involvement due to IgA deposition. Systemic lupus erythematosus presents with different systemic features and autoantibody profiles.

qs.q: A 10-year-old child presents with chronic renal failure, haematuria, partial lipodystrophy, and retinal drusen. Serology confirms markedly low serum C3. What specific immunohistochemical finding distinguishes this patient's glomerular disease from MPGN Type I?
o: Granular subendothelial deposits of IgG along capillary loops
Dense linear staining of the glomerular basement membrane
Presence of C3 staining alone without IgG, C1q, or C4
Positive staining for polyclonal IgG4 and kappa light chains
qs.e: Dense deposit disease features C3 staining alone on immunofluorescence without IgG, C1q, or C4, which clearly distinguishes it from MPGN Type I where immune complexes yield IgG and C1q deposition. The presence of C3 alone reflects alternative pathway dysregulation rather than classical immune complex deposition.
qs.s: FSGS & HIV Nephropathy: Causes, Symptoms, Diagnosis & Prognosis: MCQs
